claim: FrugalGPT (Chen, Zaharia, Zou; arXiv 2305.05176, May 2023) reports a learned LLM cascade matching GPT-4 with up to 98% cost reduction, or +4% accuracy at equal cost.
quote: Our experiments show that FrugalGPT can match the performance of the best individual LLM (e.g. GPT-4) with up to 98% cost reduction or improve the accuracy over GPT-4 by 4% with the same cost.
why: Canonical cheap-first cascade with headline cost/quality numbers; note benchmarks are 2023 API pricing, not curation tasks.

claim: RouteLLM (LMSYS, July 2024) routers cut cost by over 85% on MT Bench, 45% on MMLU and 35% on GSM8K vs GPT-4-only while keeping 95% of GPT-4 performance.
quote: cost reductions of over 85% on MT Bench, 45% on MMLU, and 35% on GSM8K as compared to using only GPT-4, while still achieving 95% of GPT-4's performance.
why: Reported cost/quality numbers for strong/weak routing; savings vary 35-85% by task.

claim: RouteLLM routers trained only on Arena data performed near-random on out-of-distribution MMLU until ~1,500 in-domain golden-label samples were added.
quote: on MMLU in Figure 4, all routers perform poorly at a near-random level when trained only on the Arena dataset, which we attribute to most MMLU questions being out-of-distribution. However, augmenting the training dataset using golden-label data
why: Evidence that routing thresholds/routers do not transfer across domains without a small in-domain labelled set - supports calibrating on our own research cards.

claim: Cascaded Selective Evaluation (Jung et al., arXiv 2407.18370, July 2024) uses cheap judges first, escalates only when confidence is low, and guarantees >80% human agreement with ~80% coverage using Mistral-7B.
quote: we propose Cascaded Selective Evaluation, where we use cheaper models as initial judges and escalate to stronger models only when necessary -- again, while still providing a provable guarantee of human agreement.
why: Closest published analogue to a cheap-scorer-then-escalate curator with a calibrated abstain/escalate threshold and agreement guarantee.

claim: UCCI (arXiv 2605.18796, May 2026) calibrates a router's confidence with isotonic regression and cuts cost 31% (95% CI 27-35%) at micro-F1 0.91 on 75,000 production queries, beating split-conformal and FrugalGPT-style thresholds.
quote: UCCI cuts inference cost by 31% (95% CI: [27%, 35%]) at micro-F1 = 0.91 while reducing ECE from 0.12 to 0.03. At the same operating point, UCCI beats entropy thresholding, split-conformal routing, and a FrugalGPT-style learned threshold.
why: Recent production-measured cascade numbers and argument that uncalibrated confidence needs per-workload threshold tuning; preprint, not yet peer reviewed.

claim: Rational Tuning of LLM Cascades (arXiv 2501.09345, Jan 2025) tunes cascade confidence thresholds via a Markov-copula probabilistic model and reports better error-cost trade-offs than Bayesian-optimisation threshold search.
quote: a framework for rationally tuning the confidence thresholds of a LLM cascade using continuous optimization. Compared to selecting confidence thresholds using Bayesian optimization, our parametric Markov-copula model yields more favorable error-cost trade-offs
why: Method for choosing escalation thresholds in a multi-stage cascade; probably heavier than needed for a 2-stage curator.

claim: Angelopoulos & Bates' conformal prediction guide recommends about n=1000 calibration points, and its Table 1 says 22 points give +/-0.10 coverage slack and 102 give +/-0.05 (alpha=0.1, delta=0.1).
quote: choosing $n=1000$ calibration points leads to coverage that is typically between $.88$ and $.92$ , hence our rough guideline of choosing about $1000$ calibration points.
why: Gives a principled answer to 'how many labels are enough' when setting a conformal keep/drop threshold; ~100 labels gives +/-5% coverage slack.

claim: Monte Carlo sizing in a practitioner post says ~200 paired labels give a 95% CI width of 0.10 on Cohen's kappa around 0.6, and ~400 around kappa 0.4, while N=50 is only tight near kappa 0.9.
quote: if your judge has Cohen's kappa around 0.6 against humans and you want a 95% confidence interval no wider than 0.10, you need approximately 200 paired labels. If your judge has kappa around 0.4, you need approximately 400.
why: Label-count guidance for measuring agreement between two judges (Jev vs Claude, or judge vs human); anonymous blog, numbers from simulation.

claim: Potato (Univ. of Michigan) annotation guide says to compare judge-human Cohen's kappa against human-human kappa rather than a fixed cutoff, with 0.8+ to rely on and 0.67-0.8 for tentative conclusions.
quote: There is no fixed threshold. Compare the judge-human kappa with the kappa between two humans on the same items. A judge close to the human-human figure agrees with people about as well as another annotator would.
why: How to interpret kappa between two judges; ties the agreement target to human ceiling. Also warns a 50-item kappa has a wide CI.

claim: A class-imbalance caveat: 50 stratified labels pin kappa to about +/-0.10-0.15 for balanced binary labels, but a 6% rare class needs 200+ (about 20/0.06 > 300 raw samples for 20 minority examples).
quote: If you need 20 examples of a 6 percent class, you need roughly 20 / 0.06, over 300 traces of raw sampling, or you oversample the rare class deliberately and weight afterward.
why: Keep/drop labels for research cards will be imbalanced (most kept or most dropped); sizing must follow the minority class. Same anonymous author as Q4-08.

claim: Jev docs page (jev-1.13.0) advises pinning a model version so calibrated thresholds do not shift, and using confidence/probabilities to auto-handle easy cases and escalate uncertain ones.
quote: Pin a model version in production so calibrated thresholds don't shift under you. - Use `confidence` / `probabilities` to auto-handle easy cases and escalate the uncertain ones.
why: Direct TypeSafe-side guidance on thresholding Jev. Domain jevtypesafeai.com may not be the official TypeSafe host (its judge page references 'the official' typesafe.ai endpoint) - gatherer should verify against Q1.

claim: The Jev-as-a-judge page says Jev's confidence is RLCD-calibrated ('a 0.9 verdict holds up about nine times in ten') but should still be calibrated against your own labelled data, and shows a 0.85 confidence cutoff for auto-apply.
quote: Treat it as calibrated but not a certificate. RLCD trains the probabilities to match real outcomes, so you can threshold on them — but you should still calibrate your cut-off against your own labelled data.
why: Vendor-side calibration claim plus example threshold 0.85; its code sample uses options/levels/.key fields that differ from the docs' criteria/choice schema, so treat as marketing, not contract.

claim: jevwiki.ai (updated 2026-09-27, jev-1.13.0) reports Jev confidence approximates clamp((n*max(p)-1)/(n-1),0,1) from a 2026-09-21 docs demo, so it ignores the runner-up gap; docs example cutoffs range 0.5-0.9 and are not defaults.
quote: The practical consequence: `confidence` depends only on the largest probability and the number of outcomes. It does not distinguish a runner-up at 0.35 from two runners-up at 0.175 each.
why: Key detail for choosing a keep/drop rule on Jev: a binary keep/drop as Noul has no confidence field (threshold noul directly with two cutoffs); confidence depends on option count. Third-party wiki citing raw TypeSafe docs.

claim: MrJev guide recommends a three-band policy (auto-act above a high cutoff, review in the middle, hand off below a low cutoff) and says to use 0.8 only as a placeholder until thresholds are measured with a coverage/accuracy sweep.
quote: A useful default shape is three bands: act automatically above the high cutoff, ask for confirmation or review in the middle, and hand off to a person or an LLM below the low cutoff.
why: Concrete keep/review/drop banding for a Jev-scored curator; third-party site, unverified.
